description: As software development students with a strong background in data analysis and web design, we are eager to apply our knowledge in this project in order to build an innovative solution to this matter.
summary:
Regolith is an interactive, data-driven tool to find analog locations on Earth that share selected physical terrain characteristics with lunar and Martian reference sites.

By combining scientific datasets, geospatial processing, and a K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) search framework, Regolith transforms complex multidimensional comparisons into interpretable similarity rankings. The current prototype analyzes four physical variables (bulk density, internal friction angle, cohesion, and regional slope) across 20 lunar and Martian reference cases and over  177,000 terrestrial candidates from Mexico and the Atacama Desert.

Through an interactive web application, users can explore potential planetary analogs.
details:
From Multidimensional Complexity to a single magnitude.

Determining the most suitable terrestrial analog for a location on the Moon or Mars requires a multivariable analysis. This presents two fundamental challenges.

The first is visualization and interpretation. When an analysis involves more than three variables, representing and comparing objects becomes increasingly difficult because the problem extends beyond the dimensions that can be directly visualized.

The second challenge is the potentially extensive number of variables that may influence terrain similarity. Depending on the purpose of the analysis, different physical, geological, thermal, or environmental characteristics may need to be considered, in other words, we are dealing with a potentially infinite number of dimensions.

Regolith addresses these challenges by implementing the KNN (nearest neighbors) approach. One of the main advantages of this algorithm is its ability to summarize differences across multiple variables through a single easily-interpretable metric: standardized Euclidean distance.

To demonstrate this approach, Regolith integrates scientific information from Earth, the Moon, and Mars through geospatial processing and data standardization.

The current prototype compares four physical characteristics: bulk density, internal friction angle, cohesion, and regional terrain slope.

Regolith combines NASADEM terrain data, SoilGrids soil properties, Landsat imagery processed through Google Earth Engine, lunar data from LOLA and Diviner, Martian data from MOLA and TES, and published planetary geotechnical information.

Terrestrial datasets were constructed for two distinct regions: a study area in Mexico and the Atacama Desert in Chile.

The resulting prototype includes 20 planetary reference cases and 177,015 environmentally screened terrestrial candidates.

Regolith was developed primarily in Python, using a combination of scientific computing, geospatial processing, machine learning, and web development technologies. Emphasizing:

  1. NumPy: Numerical computations and mathematical operations.
  2. Pandas: Data cleaning, processing, and integration of planetary datasets.
  3. Rasterio: Geospatial raster processing, reprojection, resampling, and terrain data extraction.
  4. PyProj: Geographic coordinate transformations and projection management.
  5. Scikit-learn: Feature standardization and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) similarity search.
  6. Streamlit: Development of the interactive web application.
  7. Altair: Data visualization and robustness analysis charts.
  8. Joblib: Saving and loading trained model components.

Using Landsat 8 and Landsat 9 imagery processed through Google Earth Engine, we calculated the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and the Normalized Difference Moisture Index (NDMI).

For the current prototype, we also filtered terrestrial candidates using the following criteria:

  • NDVI ≤ 0.20: To prioritize areas with relatively low vegetation signals.
  • NDMI ≤ 0.10: To prioritize areas with selected low moisture-related spectral signals.

These criteria reduced the initial terrestrial datasets to 177,015 candidate locations across Mexico and the Atacama Desert.

In the later stages of Regolith development, AI tools were used to support code review, debugging and optimization, data analysis and interpretation, as well as translation review.

This project not only aims to create a powerful and useful tool for identifying planetary analogs, but also to make complex scientific analysis more accessible and understandable. By transforming multidimensional data into intuitive visualizations and interpretable results, Regolith seeks to bridge the gap between computational methods and those who wish to explore and understand the physical similarities between Earth, the Moon, and Mars.

Regolith has the potential to scale to much larger datasets, additional geographic regions, and a wider range of physical characteristics. Its flexible nearest-neighbor framework allows the analysis to expand without fundamentally changing its methodology.
